title: South Korea Value Creators Report 2026: A Wake-Up Call for Undervalued Companies
gist: BCG's 2026 South Korea Value Creators study finds the KOSPI tripled between end-2024 and May 2026 on government reform and AI-driven semiconductor, defense, shipbuilding and nuclear-power momentum, yet over 60% of listed Korean firms still trade below book value; a durable rerating now depends on broader corporate capital discipline, following a playbook similar to Japan's post-2014 Hitachi and Dai Nippon Printing turnarounds.

insights.claim: South Korea's KOSPI index tripled between the end of 2024 and May 2026, driven by government reform, AI-fueled semiconductor demand, and rising momentum in defense, shipbuilding, and nuclear power.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Signals South Korea entering an early-stage market rerating; investors should reassess long-held 'Korea Discount' underweight positions.
insights.quote: The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) tripled between the end of 2024 and May 2026, lifted by government reform, AI-fueled semiconductor demand, and rising momentum in defense, shipbuilding, and nuclear power.
insights.locator: Sector Momentum and Policy Reform Lift Performance

insights.claim: The KOSPI's total shareholder return in 2025 reached approximately 76%, far exceeding the roughly 22% average across the top ten global indices, with almost all of that return coming from share-price appreciation rather than dividends.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: The rally so far is a re-rating of expectations, not yet a cash-return story; investors should watch whether dividend/buyback growth follows to confirm durability.
insights.quote: The KOSPI's total shareholder return (TSR) reached approximately 76%, far exceeding the roughly 22% average across the top ten global indices.
insights.locator: Sector Momentum and Policy Reform Lift Performance

insights.claim: The KOSPI's average price-to-book ratio rose from 0.8x in 2024 to 1.4x at end-2025 and is expected to reach 1.9x in 2026, while market expectations for return on equity jumped from 7.0% (2024) and 7.7% (2025) to 22% in 2026, projected to sustain into 2027.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: The valuation re-rating is tracking a steep jump in expected ROE; if actual corporate ROE delivery falls short of the 22% forecast, the multiple expansion could reverse.
insights.locator: Sector Momentum and Policy Reform Lift Performance

insights.claim: More than 60% of listed South Korean companies still trade below book value despite the broader market rally.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: The headline index rally masks a large pool of still-undervalued stocks; stock-picking rather than broad index exposure is likely to capture the next leg of the story.
insights.quote: More than 60% of listed South Korean firms still trade below book value.
insights.locator: The Rerating Remains Incomplete

insights.claim: Total KOSPI market capitalization grew roughly threefold versus 2024, with semiconductors and hardware market cap growing roughly fivefold and shipbuilding, defense, and nuclear power each growing three- to sixfold, while financials, autos, health care, consumer goods, and media/entertainment saw market cap gains of less than twofold with limited profitability improvement.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: The rally is heavily concentrated in four sectors; laggard sectors (financials, autos, health care, consumer, media) represent either value traps or catch-up candidates depending on execution.
insights.locator: Sector Momentum and Policy Reform Lift Performance

insights.claim: Outside the four leading sectors (semiconductors, shipbuilding, defense, nuclear power), average ROE in South Korea stands at around 7%, below the roughly 10% cost of equity most investors would require, meaning the typical non-leading-sector business is not generating even the minimum return shareholders expect.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: By BCG's own cost-of-equity benchmark, most of the Korean market outside four hot sectors is value-destructive on a risk-adjusted basis, a red flag for passive broad-market exposure.
insights.quote: Outside the four leading sectors, average ROE stands at around 7%—below the roughly 10% cost of equity most investors would require.
insights.locator: The Rerating Remains Incomplete

insights.claim: Despite the rally, South Korea's estimated 2026 price-to-book ratio of 1.9x remains below that of the US, Taiwan, India, and Europe, indicating the rerating is still incomplete relative to global peers.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: A persistent valuation gap versus global peers suggests further multiple-expansion room if broader corporate reform materializes, a relative-value case for continued Korea overweight.
insights.quote: Despite the recent rally, however, South Korea’s estimated 2026 PBR of 1.9x remains below that of the US, Taiwan, India, and Europe.
insights.locator: The Rerating Remains Incomplete

insights.claim: The first wave of South Korea's rerating was driven by two forces: earnings momentum in semiconductors, shipbuilding, defense, and nuclear power, and government reforms including Commercial law amendments, the Corporate Value-Up Program, dividend tax reforms, and proposed restrictions on value-destructive corporate structures.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Investors should separate sector-earnings beta from policy-driven structural change when assessing which gains are durable versus cyclical.
insights.locator: Sector Momentum and Policy Reform Lift Performance

insights.claim: South Korea's reforms target the institutional roots of the valuation gap by expanding directors' fiduciary duties to all shareholders, strengthening audit committee independence, encouraging disclosure, incentivizing dividends, and tightening scrutiny of dual listings.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: These specific governance levers (fiduciary duty scope, dual-listing scrutiny) are trackable milestones for gauging whether reform momentum is being sustained or stalling.
insights.locator: Sector Momentum and Policy Reform Lift Performance

insights.claim: BCG frames the first wave of South Korea's rerating as 'a beginning, not an endpoint,' arguing a sustainable rerating requires broader corporate action beyond the four leading sectors to improve ROE, allocate capital more effectively, and deliver consistent shareholder value.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: The core investment thesis: favor companies executing capital discipline over passive exposure to sector beta, since the current rally is not self-sustaining without broader corporate follow-through.
insights.quote: the first wave of South Korea’s rerating should be seen as a beginning, not an endpoint.
insights.locator: The Rerating Remains Incomplete

themes.theme: Why TSR is no longer optional

insights.claim: South Korean household wealth has historically been concentrated in real estate and other illiquid assets, but policy efforts are increasingly shifting capital toward equities, and the number of domestic retail investors has risen sharply as a result.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Rising retail equity ownership creates a structural, socially-reinforced constituency pressuring corporates to sustain shareholder returns, an underappreciated tailwind for continued reform.
insights.quote: Household assets have historically been concentrated in real estate and other illiquid assets, but policy efforts are increasingly aimed at shifting more capital toward equities.
insights.locator: Why TSR Improvement Is No Longer Optional

insights.claim: Shareholder activism in South Korea is becoming more forceful, with activists increasingly willing to push for board changes, executive replacement, portfolio restructuring, and asset sales, beyond simply demanding higher dividends.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Companies with weak TSR and bloated non-core portfolios are increasingly activist targets, a catalyst worth monitoring for event-driven trades.
insights.quote: Activists are increasingly willing to push for board changes, executive replacement, portfolio restructuring, and asset sales.
insights.locator: Why TSR Improvement Is No Longer Optional

insights.claim: Over the past decade, South Korean aggregate net income grew at a solid pace, but ROE barely improved because excess cash, non-core assets, and continued investment in low-return businesses diluted returns.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Earnings growth alone does not justify a rerating; investors should screen Korean holdings for capital-allocation discipline rather than top-line growth alone.
insights.quote: Over the past decade, aggregate net income grew at a solid pace. But ROE barely improved, as excess cash, non-core assets, and continued investment in low-return businesses diluted returns.
insights.locator: Why TSR Improvement Is No Longer Optional

insights.claim: Starting in 2014 under the Abe administration, Japan spent a decade reshaping corporate capital management, governance, and investor relations; net income growth was similar to South Korea's, but ROE improved far more because Japanese companies restructured non-core businesses, expanded dividends, bought back and canceled shares, and managed against cost-of-capital expectations, and the market rewarded that shift with a sustained rerating.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Japan's decade-long reform cycle is the template BCG expects South Korea to compress into a few years; the specific levers (buybacks with cancellation, cost-of-capital discipline) are what to look for in Korean corporate actions.
insights.quote: The Japanese restructured non-core businesses, expanded dividends, bought back and canceled shares, and increasingly managed against cost-of-capital expectations. The market rewarded that shift with a sustained rerating.
insights.locator: Learning from Japan’s Experience

insights.claim: Hitachi simplified its business structure, exited more than 20 listed subsidiaries, refocused around core digital infrastructure, and strengthened board independence; its ROE improved from -29% in 2009 to 14% in 2022, and its stock rose approximately 5.5x during the transformation period and nearly 20x from its 2009 level by early May 2026.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent showing portfolio simplification plus governance reform can drive a multi-decade, multi-bagger re-rating, a comparable playbook for Korean conglomerates with complex subsidiary structures.
insights.quote: ROE improved from –29% in 2009 to 14% in 2022.
insights.locator: Learning from Japan’s Experience

insights.claim: Dai Nippon Printing made capital efficiency an explicit priority in 2023, setting public targets of ROE of at least 10% and PBR above 1x, shifted its portfolio from mature printing toward semiconductors and displays, and executed approximately ¥300 billion in share buybacks; ROE rose from a decade-long average of 3.2% before the announcement to an average of 8.3% afterward, and its stock has risen approximately 2.6x since early 2023.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Shows that publicly announced, numeric capital-efficiency targets combined with large buybacks can rapidly re-rate even a legacy, mature business within about two years.
insights.quote: ROE rose from a decade-long average of 3.2% before the announcement to an average of 8.3% afterward.
insights.locator: Learning from Japan’s Experience

insights.claim: Hyundai Elevator used overseas business restructuring as a starting point, then raised its dividend payout ratio to an average of approximately 150% over the past two years, improving its ROE from 14% to 20%.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: A domestic proof-of-concept that combining an operational fix with aggressive capital return can lift ROE meaningfully; a template for identifying similar re-rating candidates in Korea.
insights.quote: it raised its dividend payout ratio to an average of approximately 150% over the past two years, and in the process improved ROE from 14% to 20%.
insights.locator: A South Korean Transformation

insights.claim: JB Financial Group paired profitability management (targeting niche customer segments, expanding net interest margins, improving loan loss ratios) with active share buybacks, delivering five consecutive years of about 12% ROE, among the strongest levels for South Korean financial holding companies.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Even within financials, a laggard sector overall in this rally, execution-driven outliers exist; a potential differentiated pick versus sector-wide underperformance.
insights.quote: five consecutive years of about 12% in ROE—among the strongest levels for South Korean financial holding companies
insights.locator: A South Korean Transformation

themes.theme: The playbook for the next wave

insights.claim: BCG argues South Korean businesses must shift their aspiration from being a 'great company' to becoming a 'great stock,' since operational strength alone is no longer enough without demonstrated capital efficiency, shareholder returns, and market confidence.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Reframes stock-selection criteria for Korea-focused investors: filter for capital-efficiency and shareholder-return signals, not just operating performance.
insights.quote: from being a “great company” to becoming a “great stock.”
insights.locator: What Companies Must Do Now to Improve TSR

insights.claim: BCG's recommended business-strategy move is portfolio discipline: identify which businesses and assets earn returns above the cost of capital versus which should be restructured, sold, or monetized, and review whether dual listings or complex ownership structures continue to serve shareholders.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Investors can screen Korean conglomerates for portfolio complexity and dual-listing discounts as potential catalysts for restructuring-driven re-rating.
insights.locator: What Companies Must Do Now to Improve TSR

insights.claim: BCG recommends using return on invested capital (ROIC) versus weighted average cost of capital (WACC) as a core investment decision metric, since investments earning below WACC destroy value even if they add revenue or accounting profit, and should be tracked with post-investment monitoring.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete lens (ROIC vs WACC) for evaluating the quality of Korean corporate capex and M&A decisions going forward.
insights.quote: Investments that cannot earn returns above weighted average cost of capital (WACC) destroy value, even if they add revenue or accounting profit.
insights.locator: What Companies Must Do Now to Improve TSR

insights.claim: BCG recommends companies either pursue attractive reinvestment opportunities or return excess capital to shareholders through predictable dividends, buybacks, and treasury share cancellation, guided by a clear multiyear payout policy, since investors value shareholder return policies they can understand and underwrite.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Watch for Korean companies announcing multiyear, transparent payout policies as a signal reducing valuation discount risk.
insights.quote: Investors value shareholder return policies they can understand and underwrite.
insights.locator: What Companies Must Do Now to Improve TSR

insights.claim: BCG argues companies need a clear equity story that answers 'why invest here,' tying business strategy, capital allocation, shareholder returns, and specific financial targets together, elevating investor relations into a CEO-level, cross-functional strategic capability rather than a disclosure function.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Quality and credibility of a company's equity-story communication becomes an investable differentiator among otherwise similar re-rating candidates.
insights.quote: companies need a clear equity story that answers the question, Why invest here?
insights.locator: What Companies Must Do Now to Improve TSR

insights.claim: BCG recommends executive compensation be linked not just to revenue or operating profit but also to ROE, TSR, and long-term value creation, so that management incentives align with shareholder outcomes.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/joonho-lee
insights.so_what: Executive comp structure disclosure becomes a due-diligence checkpoint for assessing whether a Korean company's management is truly incentivized to close the valuation gap.
insights.quote: Executive compensation should be linked to not just revenue or operating profit, but also to ROE, TSR, and long-term value creation.
insights.locator: What Companies Must Do Now to Improve TSR
